newsitem.title: UK: Independent traders cram into hectic Euroswiss pit.
newsitem.headline: Independent traders cram into hectic Euroswiss pit.

text.p: Independent traders are squeezing into London's tiny Euroswiss futures trading pit to capitalise on market anxiety over European monetary union, traders and analysts said on Monday.

The traders, known as locals, make money from trading in and out of fast-moving contracts. The Swiss franc's status as a safe haven currency for European economic and monetary union (EMU) has turned the three-month money market future into a local's dream.
The Euroswiss future listed on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) posted record turnover of 418,953 contracts in May, and 387,189 in April.

June volume looks set to break another high. The market has been active following a statement from the Swiss National Bank (SNB) on May 21 that it would act to counter the Swiss franc's rise, after the currency hit a seven-month high against the mark.

The Euroswiss futures contract traded 279,492 lots in the month to date. Euroswiss options, which have recorded sky-high implied volatility levels, had traded a more meagre 3,226 contracts by mid-month.

"The bottom line is that the Swiss government wants to inject liquidity into the market. That's brought the Swiss banks in, and now the locals have come in," said local Terence Walshe as he jostled for space in the teeming pit with other locals wearing plain red jackets, and bank and brokerage employees in more patterned designs.
The Euroswiss pit is dwarfed on the crowded LIFFE floor by the Bund and gilt trading areas.
But the Swiss National Bank's actions over recent weeks have weaned traders away from more traditional markets, analysts said.

The SNB has been offering liquidity, in the form of sight deposits, at levels below current official Swiss interest rates of 1.50 percent. Swiss banks have been hedging their positions with the Euroswiss contract, traders said.
The central bank's actions are designed to curb the rise in the Swiss franc because of fears a stronger currency could aggravate already gloomy economic outlook.
The currency has benefited from its safe haven status as European Union leaders grapple with agreement on the introduction of a single currency.
"The Swiss economy is showing only tentative signs of recovery," said Julian Callow, European economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.
International investors traditionally find it difficult to access Swiss bonds, because of the small size of the market, analysts said.
There has been greater international interest in the sector recently.
"Some institutions have been buying Swiss franc bonds as a safe haven, and the currency strength reflects that buying," said Andrew Davies, bond analyst at London Bond Broking.
But low-yielding Swiss bonds have to compete with other more appealing safe haven markets such as gilts and U.S. Treasuries, and have limited appeal, analysts added.
"Ten-year yields are at 3.35 percent -- that's almost as low as Japan," said Callow.

As a result, Euroswiss futures volumes are likely to remain small, analysts said, when compared with Bunds or Euromarks, which in May traded 3.8 million and 2.3 million contracts on LIFFE respectively.
